newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia dlr undermined by the profit motive.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia dlr undermined by the profit motive.

text.p: The Australian dollar was forced to surrender some hard won gains Thursday as offshore profit taking snapped support and triggered stop loss sales.

Traders said both U.S. and Japanese banks began cashing in long AUD/yen positions when the local unit failed to sustain a break above 89.00 yen this morning. That snowballed when rumours circulated a U.S. investment bank had issued a bearish note on the currency, although this proved hard to track down.
"It's been a combination of things," said Steve North, chief dealer corporate forex at Chase. "But essentially the market was long and needed a good cleanse out. It's pretty much over now."
By 5.00 pm (0700 GMT) the dollar had sagged to US$0.7919/24 from an early US$0.7946/51 and US$0.7935/40 Wednesday.
Support was pegged at US$0.7910, which North expected to hold in the near term, while resistance had now firmly established itself at US$0.7965.

On the crosses, it drifted off to 88.47/57 yen from Wednesday's strong 88.88/98 finish, that had been a four year high for the currency. In trade weighted terms it was back at its previous 58.7 close having come near to a five year peak of 59.00 this morning. It also briefly touched three month highs on the Swiss franc and German mark.
The dollar's lapse was attributed in part to talk U.S. investment bank Merrill Lynch had issued a report calling the currency down to 77 cents in the next couple of months.

This should not have been a surprise, however, as the bank has been bearish for some time. In a Reuter consensus survey on the dollar carried out in August, for instance, Merrill's economist Nigel Douglas was already looking for 77 cents by year-end.
"The whole episode smacks of a useful excuse to sell," said North at Chase Australia. "Anyway, plenty of other people are not comfortable with the AUD up near 80 cents."

One of those was Michael Blythe, a currency economist at Comonwealth Bank, who had issued a note today revising down his forecast for the dollar to 77.00 cents by year end from a previously expected 79.00 cents.
"We have revised down our two month target on the back of lower commodity prices, monetary policy perceptions, current account trends and possible Senate budget delays," he said.

Blythe reckoned the market had yet to factor in the effect of the weaker trend in commodity prices on Australia's export earnings or or the risk of the current account deficit widening from the unusually low levels of recent months.

The CBA team also warned that another cut in Australian interest rates could not be ruled out. They attached a 40 percent probability to such an easing, which was actually a lot more cautious than many analysts and the money market here.
The 90-day bank bill future contract for December stands at 93.43, implying a rate of 6.57 percent compared to the present official rate of 7.00 percent.

Finally, Blythe saw potential trouble with the passage of the government's tough 1996/97 budget through the Senate, where it is in a minority and needs the cooperation of minor parties who, so far, have been hostile to some of the measures.
However, CBA remained bullish on the longer term prospects for the currency given the potential for greater synchronisation in global economic activity next year.
Stronger growth in major economies could only be beneficial for commodity prices in general and the local dollar in particular, Blythe said.

"Any period of weakness should be relatively short lived," he said. "On this basis we continue to advise buying on dips, with a view to benefiting from a steady appreciation of the AUD through 1997." He saw the currency reaching the low 80 cent area by the middle of next year. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
